extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO OED (patent attorneys/agents) and counsel handling USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Administrative/judicial standards applied in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) disciplinary proceedings evaluating allegations such as commingling, failure to refund unearned fees, neglect of client matters, recordkeeping, and general professional misconduct under 37 C.F.R. rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client funds vs. fees paid in advance (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.112 and 10.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: The monies that clients paid were 'funds' belonging to these clients and not belonging to Respondent and 'fees paid in advance' that had not been earned by Respondent, as described in 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.112 and 10.40.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fee agreement that does not specify what happens to monies if never earned, does not state the fee is a nonrefundable retainer, and does not show informed consent that fees are earned on receipt means the monies are client funds/advance fees and not the practitioner's upon receipt. Prior USPTO and court decisions reject the contention that advance fees immediately belong to the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit and maintenance of advance fees in a separate account (37 C.F.R. § 10.112(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must deposit and maintain advance fees from clients in a separate account until earned and due; failure to do so is commingling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositing client advance-fee checks into a general checking account used for personal and business transactions violates 37 C.F.R. § 10.112(a),(b). Expert testimony explains that the Rules require keeping practitioner's money separate from client money not yet earned; case facts (depositing Ms. Chess's and Mr. Sprague's checks into a personal Wachovia account) illustrate commingling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commingling prohibition (37 C.F.R. § 10.112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing client funds (advance fees not yet earned) with the practitioner's personal funds constitutes commingling and is prohibited under 37 C.F.R. § 10.112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must avoid placing client monies into accounts used for personal withdrawals/payments. The USPTO Rules, not state rules, govern representation before the USPTO; narrow state exceptions (e.g., informed consent) do not excuse commingling absent compliance with USPTO Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and accounting for client funds (37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain complete records of all funds of clients that come into their possession and must render appropriate accounting to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to maintain complete records and to render accounting for client funds (advance fees) violates 37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(3). The decision finds such failures by clear and convincing evidence where records were incomplete or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt refund/return of unearned fees upon withdrawal (37 C.F.R. § 10.40(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lawyer and client separate, the lawyer must promptly return property belonging to the client that is in the lawyer's possession and the client is entitled to receive (37 C.F.R. § 10.40(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rules do not define 'prompt'—it is determined case-by-case based on facts. Expert testimony can inform what is 'prompt' in context (e.g., returning Ms. Chess's full $2,300 on a promised date). Failure to promptly refund unearned advance fees upon withdrawal is a violation (example: not returning refunds despite repeated client requests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of an entrusted legal matter / failure to act competently (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) and § 10.77(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect of an entrusted legal matter includes failing to prosecute a matter in a timely manner, failing to act competently by handling a legal matter without adequate preparation, and failing to timely and adequately communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.77(c), 10.77(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of neglect/competence failures: not completing work promised (e.g., six‑week promise to complete a patent application but never working on it); failing to respond to repeated client inquiries; missing deadlines; not taking action within time frames set with the client. Expert guidance cited: standard telephone response time ~24 hours, email even faster; diligent lawyers respond very promptly. Such conduct, established by clear and convincing evidence, constitutes violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct; conduct adversely reflecting on ability to practice (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct or conduct that adversely reflects on a practitioner's ability to practice before the USPTO is prohibited (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general disciplinary standard used to assess whether particular acts (e.g., commingling, failure to refund, neglect, poor client communication) amount to disreputable or gross misconduct. The opinion references prior ALJ/Commissioner/District Court/Federal Circuit decisions upholding suspensions and findings under these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent / explicit fee agreement language for nonrefundable retainers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance fees can be treated as nonrefundable or as earned upon receipt only if the fee agreement expressly states that or the client gives informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fee agreement lacking language that the fee is nonrefundable or that fees are earned on receipt (with informed client consent) means the advance fee remains client property until earned. The absence of such provisions was dispositive in finding the monies were client funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for disciplinary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings of violations in this disciplinary proceeding are made by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision repeatedly notes that violations (e.g., failure to refund, neglect, commingling) were found 'by clear and convincing evidence.' Parties should expect this evidentiary standard in determinations of professional misconduct in similar proceedings.
